summary:
unior Astronaut Mission Trainer (Proyecto Ares-IV) is an interactive resource management and survival video game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, tailored for children aged 7 to 12

The project translates authentic NASA aerospace engineering datasets and life-support systems—such as ECLSS, WRS, and Kilopower reactors—into gamified space missions across lunar and Martian environments. Rather than relying on arbitrary currency, the game incorporates NASA’s Equivalent System Mass (ESM) metric, requiring players to balance mass, volume, power, and crew time while managing five critical survival variables: electricity, water, food, health, and oxygen. Players navigate realistic engineering trade-offs and forced sacrifices during emergency scenarios like solar flares or power eclipses.

This simulation addresses the critical STEM engagement window (ages 10–12) by converting abstract aerospace concepts and environmental stewardship into engaging, inquiry-based gameplay. By demonstrating that "what is not measured gets depleted," it connects off-world resource management directly to conserving resources on Earth, inspiring the next generation of scientists and engineers.
details:
Ares-IV: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an innovative, web-based strategy and resource-management video game specifically created for children aged 7 to 12. Players step into the role of Mission Commander supervising a pioneering space expedition to either the Moon or Mars. Grounded in authentic NASA aerospace engineering principles, the core gameplay focuses on managing five vital survival metrics across daily solar cycles: Electricity, Water, Food, Oxygen, and Crew Health. Rather than relying on simplified in-game currency, the simulation integrates NASA's official Equivalent System Mass framework, requiring players to balance physical constraints including mass, volume, power, and crew work hours. As daily automatic consumption occurs based on crew composition, commanders select daily operational priorities while confronting realistic environmental challenges—such as eclipse voltage drops, solar flares, and air filter saturations—that force strategic trade-offs to keep the crew alive.
The project delivers extensive benefits by cultivating critical thinking, strategic planning, leadership, and decision-making skills under realistic physical constraints. By reaching children during the critical STEM affinity window between ages 10 and 12, the game sparks early interest in aerospace engineering, astrophysics, space agronomy, and medicine before academic choices consolidate. It translates complex aerospace technologies—such as water recovery systems, Sabatier reactors, and solar arrays—into intuitive visual metaphors that preserve scientific accuracy while remaining accessible. Furthermore, the game promotes real-world environmental awareness by teaching young players that closed-loop survival in space directly mirrors the urgent need for resource conservation on Earth.
The overarching objective of the project is to democratize high-quality space and STEM education worldwide, ensuring that interactive learning tools are accessible regardless of geographic or socio-economic background. By connecting foundational classroom concepts to authentic space exploration challenges, the game actively combats the drop-off in scientific interest among young students. Through engaging storytelling and realistic simulation mechanics, the project aims to broaden the global pipeline of future engineers, scientists, and astronauts who will push the boundaries of human space exploration.
To bring the game to life, the team developed the core logic and web interactivity using Phaser JS alongside modular JavaScript. All visual assets, user interface components, dashboards, character avatars, and system icons were fully handcrafted using Figma to create crisp, high-resolution vector artwork. The underlying simulation models are grounded in official NASA open-science datasets and technical documentation, including the DONKI Space Weather API for solar radiation events and the NASA Baseline Values and Assumptions Document for life-support metrics.
Creativity is central to the project, as every graphic asset and interaction model was designed completely from scratch by the team. The game stands out as a unique entry in space-related EdTech by rejecting arbitrary arcade tropes like infinite resources or fantasy coins in favor of real physics-based constraints tailored for young minds. Its cumulative narrative engine ensures that every operational decision carries lasting consequences, reinforcing the fundamental lesson that resources in a closed system must be carefully measured and preserved.
In designing the experience, the team carefully evaluated the developmental needs of children aged 7 to 12, creating an intuitive UI/UX that treats young players with intellectual respect through clear, figurative language rather than oversimplified explanations. The mathematical design incorporates authentic break-even curves, helping players understand when to choose lightweight disposable supplies versus heavy, energy-intensive recycling machinery based on mission length. Additionally, the game encourages off-screen collaborative problem-solving by prompting kids to discuss complex space dilemmas with parents, teachers, and peers. Finally, the team structured a sustainable business model combining freemium educational access, family subscriptions, and school integration packages to maximize impact and ensure long-term scalability.
